He said yes in eleven seconds, and that was the part that should have worried
me.

We were in a room above a bike shop in Nation, three months into my first year
of doing this on my own. I had spent the weekend deciding what to charge and I
had landed on a number I could say out loud without my voice going up at the
end. I said it. He said yes before I had finished the sentence.

I walked out pleased. That lasted about six weeks, which is how long it took
for the mandate to turn into what it actually was: two board packs, a data room
that opened early, and a Sunday spent on a revenue schedule nobody had told me
existed. The number I had said out loud was a number for the work I imagined,
not the work that arrived.

I did it again on the second mandate. I did it a third time, in the same
direction, and by then it was not nerves. It was a method. I was pricing the
version of the engagement where nothing goes wrong, and no engagement is that
version.

What I changed is not the number. I raised it twice since, and that is on the
site, dated, so anyone can see the history. What I changed is what I say before
the number. I now describe the month I am selling, out loud, including the week
where the close slips and the board asks for a scenario at eleven at night. Then
I say the price.

Nobody has said yes in eleven seconds since. Two people have said no, which is
information I was not getting before.

Nadia Feriel, fractional CFO for seed and Series A B2B SaaS.
I build the model and I sit in the room when it gets argued about.
